A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MeshAnything V2 and retain matching core methods, equations, figures, and experiments. All material supports comparison: v1 ends with references, while v2 includes additional experiments and limitations in Appendices A–B.

before.justification: v1 reports original mesh-generation examples, quantitative AMT ablation results in Table 1, and an empirical token-length comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original results in Tables 1–3, including tokenization comparisons and face-count control, plus a 43-participant user study in Appendix A.2.

M1.justification: v2 extends the stated method with optional vertex swapping using a new special token, face-count conditioning through an additional embedding, and invalid-prediction masking during inference. These change tokenization, conditioning, and decoding beyond the basic AMT procedure described in v1.

E1.justification: Appendix A.1 adds evaluation under explicit requested face counts, extending the requirements of shape-conditioned mesh generation. v2 also reports including a small ObjaverseXL portion, while retaining the same mesh domain and 1,600-face limit. The smaller-face subsets used elsewhere are protocol changes within retained coverage.

E2.justification: v1's quantitative comparison uses V2 and its no-AMT variant. v2 retains that comparison and adds Unsort, PolyGen(AMT), and AMT(Swap) in Table 2, plus a direct MeshAnything-versus-V2 user study. PolyGen(AMT) is explicitly an adapted single-model implementation combined with AMT, not unmodified PolyGen.

E3.justification: The reported corpus increases from 100K to 230K pairs, and Section 4.1 changes evaluation size from 2K to 4K, although v2 Section 4.3 still says 2K. New Table 2 experiments use OPT-125M, meshes with at most 400 faces, 10K metric-sampling points, and training perplexity. Appendix A adds face-count scaling and a preference protocol involving 30 meshes and 43 users. The main ablation retains 100K metric-sampling points.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained AMT/no-AMT ablation, Table 2 tests sorting, alternative representation choices, and vertex swapping, examining regularity versus compression. Appendix A.1 adds sensitivity to requested face counts, and Appendix A.2 adds perceptual assessment through a user study.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The newly reported number of user-study participants is a study sample size, not uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces numerical results: CD values in units of 10^-2 for the no-AMT variant and V2 change from 1.454/0.802 to 0.895/0.874, alongside other metric updates. Revised data settings prevent interpreting these as same-setting performance changes. Tables 2–3 add tokenization and face-control outcomes; Appendix A.2 reports preferences of 67.8% for V2 versus 32.2% for MeshAnything.

T1.justification: Appendix A.3 adds an explicit token-cost argument comparing 3+n with 3n tokens for a vertex referenced n times. The original mesh and face definitions in Equations (1)–(3) remain mathematically equivalent, and no substantial theorem or proof framework is introduced.

C1.justification: v2 adds an explicit claim of user-controllable face counts and makes balancing compactness with sequence regularity a stated contribution. The central claims of roughly halving token length, improving efficiency and quality, and doubling capacity to 1,600 faces remain.

C2.justification: v2 develops the interpretation that compression alone is insufficient, attributing PolyGen(AMT)'s quality deficit to difficulty referencing previously generated vertices. It also interprets face-count control saturation as prioritizing mesh quality and discusses swap-related tradeoffs. These substantially expand the explanatory discussion. The industrial-readiness limitation is retained unchanged in Appendix B.

D1.justification: v2 substantially expands implementation information through coordinate-based deduplication, Chamfer-based filtering of failed mesh2sdf conversions, 10% face-condition dropout, and details of the single-model PolyGen adaptation. Hardware, four-day training duration, and batch size remain unchanged. v1's open-source statement becomes a future code/model release promise; the PDFs do not establish actual resource accessibility.

R1.justification: v2 adds three language-tokenization references and a reference supporting mesh2sdf processing, while expanding discussion of the already-cited PolyGen representation. The existing mesh-generation and general 3D-generation positioning is largely retained.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten, contributions are reordered and expanded, and the quantitative section is reorganized around metrics and tokenization comparisons. v2 introduces supplementary sections and moves the existing limitations paragraph from the combined conclusion section to Appendix B.

P2.justification: The document changes from a single-column to a two-column layout. Existing Figures 1–2 are retained but relocated and resized, and Algorithm 1 is reformatted with line numbers. Table 1 gains a sequence-ratio column, and Tables 2–3 introduce new comparison and face-control displays.

improvement.justification: v1's quantitative validation centered on one AMT/no-AMT ablation. v2's alternative-tokenization experiments directly examine the roles of compression and ordering, addressing an important gap in support for the central representation claims. Face-control tests and a direct human comparison further strengthen validation. The 4K/2K inconsistency and claims of preserved quality despite mixed Table 2 metrics remain weaknesses, but the added comparative evidence provides a substantial net improvement.
